Choose:
Build cache only: remove Rust target/ directory
Reason: target/ is generated Rust build output and safe to recreate.
Do not remove .agents/ just for hygiene. In this repo it can contain agent/skill/reference material and should be treated as source/configuration unless separately proven disposable.
Also do not select the “full hygiene sweep” unless the tool first inventories each temp/backup artifact and proves it is generated/non-authoritative.
So the safe scope is:
REMOVE:
- target/

PRESERVE:
- .agents/
- source files
- docs/reference files
- unknown temp/backup artifacts
This is the minimal hygiene change with the lowest risk.

Yes. There are mature TUI foundations you can reuse instead of building the LBE terminal UI from zero.
Best fit for LBE: OpenTUI
For your current direction, OpenTUI is the strongest fit.
It gives you:
native terminal rendering
React-style component composition through @opentui/react
flexbox layout
scrollable panes
mouse interaction
streaming markdown
syntax-highlighted diffs
dialogs/modals
keyboard handling
cross-platform terminal support
OpenTUI is already used by production terminal applications, and its own docs provide starter/example projects.
OpenTUI
+1
More importantly, the current Cline CLI already uses exactly this stack:
TypeScript
    ↓
@opentui/react
    ↓
@opentui/core
    ↓
native Zig renderer
Its CLI architecture already includes a runtime-to-TUI bridge, dialogs, model picker, tool approval UI, slash commands, autocomplete, session handling, streaming content, and E2E TUI tests.
GitHub
That makes it much closer to what LBE needs than a generic dashboard template.
What I would reuse
Not the whole Cline product/runtime.
Use its TUI implementation as a presentation/runtime-client reference:
Cline/OpenTUI mechanics
        ↓ adapt

LBE terminal shell
├─ conversation/activity view
├─ composer
├─ slash command UX
├─ provider/model selector
├─ dialogs
├─ keyboard navigation
├─ scroll/history handling
├─ streaming markdown
├─ tool-call cards
├─ diff rendering
└─ responsive terminal layout

        ↓

LBE bridge

        ↓

LBE authoritative owners
├─ sessions
├─ provider registry
├─ provider health
├─ capabilities
├─ authorization
├─ tool orchestration
├─ receipts/evidence
├─ validation
└─ completion
The crucial rule remains:
Reuse the terminal mechanics, not the authority model.
Cline itself documents that the CLI renders runtime events while its core owns agent/runtime/session persistence. For LBE, those ownership points must instead terminate at the appropriate LBE owners.
GitHub
There are also generic starters
OpenTUI itself has a starter command:
Bash
bun create tui
and ships standalone examples.
GitHub
So you have two practical choices:
Approach Suitability for LBE
OpenTUI starter/examples Good foundation, but you design most agent UX
Cline apps/cli TUI patterns Best reference for LBE agent terminal
Python Textual Technically capable, but conflicts with the direction you've now established
Ink Mature React terminal rendering, but less directly aligned with the existing Cline/OpenTUI reference
Bubble Tea Strong Go framework, but would introduce another runtime/language boundary
Other mature frameworks certainly exist—Textual, Ink, Bubble Tea, etc.—but choosing another one now would create more divergence rather than reduce it.
TermUI
My recommendation
Do not search for a random "LBE dashboard TUI template."
Use:
OpenTUI
+
selected Cline CLI interaction patterns
+
LBE-specific visual/product contract
+
LBE runtime bridge
That gives you a ready, proven terminal foundation without importing another execution authority.
And importantly, it fits the problem you identified earlier: the visual structure should be fixed first, rather than letting every agent invent a new TUI.
A sensible next artifact would therefore be a Cline/OpenTUI → LBE component reuse matrix, for example:
Cline component/pattern        LBE disposition

root layout                    ADAPT
composer                       ADAPT
autocomplete                   ADAPT
markdown activity stream       REUSE/ADAPT
diff rendering                 REUSE/ADAPT
dialogs                        REUSE
provider picker                ADAPT → LBE ProviderRegistry
session controls               ADAPT → LbeSessionService
tool approval UI               ADAPT → LBE authorization
runtime bridge                 REPLACE → LBE bridge
session persistence            REJECT as authority
execution authority            REJECT
completion authority           REJECT
branding                       REPLACE → LetterBlack
That would prevent another independent TUI implementation from appearing while still letting you reuse a large amount of mature terminal UX.

Yes. You can completely avoid using Cline as an intermediary.
The architecture you are describing is preferable for LBE if you want LetterBlack to own the provider layer rather than routing authentication and inference through another product.
What the Cline docs confirm
The model-provider documentation separates provider credentials from the agent surface. Provider configuration can contain an API key, base URL, headers, and provider-specific settings. It lists direct credentials for Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, AWS Bedrock, Mistral, and OpenAI-compatible services.
Cline
The separate Cline API is a different architecture. It deliberately acts as an aggregator:
App
 ↓
Cline API
 ↓
Anthropic / OpenAI / Google / ...
and uses one Cline API key to access multiple model providers.
Cline
You do not need that layer.
For LBE, use:
                         ┌─ OpenAI
                         ├─ Anthropic
LBE Provider Gateway ────┼─ Google Gemini
                         ├─ AWS Bedrock
                         ├─ Mistral
                         ├─ OpenAI-compatible
                         ├─ LM Studio
                         └─ Ollama
No:
LBE → Cline account → provider
and no:
LBE → api.cline.bot → provider
Recommended LBE architecture
The UI repository should only see this:
LBE TUI
   │
   ▼
LbeWrapper
   │
   ▼
LBE Runtime
   │
   ▼
LBE Provider Gateway
   │
   ├── OpenAiAdapter
   ├── AnthropicAdapter
   ├── GeminiAdapter
   ├── BedrockAdapter
   ├── MistralAdapter
   ├── OpenAiCompatibleAdapter
   ├── LmStudioAdapter
   └── OllamaAdapter
The providers connect directly to their respective platform APIs.
That makes Cline useful only as a reference implementation/documentation source, not a runtime dependency.
Already covered vs still missing
From the work we have already defined for the TUI, some provider concepts are already covered at the contract/UI level:
Area Current state
provider selection UI COVERED AS UI CONTRACT
model selection COVERED
model ID COVERED
model family COVERED
context usage COVERED
effort/reasoning projection COVERED
provider health concept DOCUMENTED
model discovery concept DOCUMENTED
provider authentication UI DOCUMENTED / MOCK
live direct provider adapters NOT IMPLEMENTED
credential storage NOT IMPLEMENTED
provider capability normalization NOT IMPLEMENTED
provider-specific streaming NOT IMPLEMENTED
provider-specific tool calling NOT IMPLEMENTED
provider error normalization NOT IMPLEMENTED
So I would not add Cline API authentication to the LBE contract.
Instead, add an explicit LBE-native provider contract.
1. ProviderId
Something like:
Rust
pub enum ProviderId {
    OpenAi,
    Anthropic,
    Gemini,
    Bedrock,
    Mistral,
    OpenAiCompatible,
    LmStudio,
    Ollama,
}
It is an LBE identifier, not a Cline provider ID.
2. Provider configuration
Use a neutral configuration:
Rust
pub struct ProviderConfig {
    pub provider_id: ProviderId,
    pub base_url: Option<String>,
    pub credential_ref: Option<String>,
    pub headers: Vec<(String, String)>,
}
Important:
credential_ref
should reference secure storage.
Do not send raw API keys through normal TUI snapshots/events.
3. Authentication should be provider-native
For example conceptually:
OpenAI
  → OpenAI API key / supported OpenAI auth

Anthropic
  → Anthropic API key

Google
  → Gemini API key / Google application credentials

AWS Bedrock
  → AWS credential chain

OpenAI-compatible
  → provider-specific API key + base URL

LM Studio
  → local endpoint

Ollama
  → local endpoint
The Cline model-provider documentation itself demonstrates this provider-specific credential approach, including environment variables and direct base URLs.
Cline

This is especially important because providers differ.
Rust

    pub tools: bool,
    pub reasoning: bool,
    pub images: bool,

There are several pieces from those API docs worth adopting as generic contracts.
Their API supports:

streaming;

Instead each provider adapter translates LBE's neutral request into its native API.

Rust

Tool calling is particularly important
The Chat Completions documentation demonstrates the standard lifecycle:

        ↓
tool_call_id
        ↓

LBE receives ToolCall
        ↓
LBE governance / approval
        ↓
LBE executes allowed capability
        ↓
result
        ↓
provider continuation
That is a critical difference.
The provider does not get execution authority.

Yes. I checked the current cline/cline repo as a reference implementation, and there are still several useful areas not yet represented in your mock UI contract.
Highest-value remaining areas
1. Runtime connection / attachment states
Cline’s SDK architecture distinguishes local in-process runtime, hub-backed runtime, detached clients, reconnect, shared sessions, and resumed sessions.
For LBE UI, add only the projection contract:
RuntimeConnectionState
- Mock
- Disconnected
- Connecting
- Connected
- Reconnecting
- Attached
- Error
and possibly:
runtime_id
runtime_mode
attached_client_count
This is useful even if the real wall remains disconnected for now.
2. Session status truth
The repo explicitly treats session status as something reported by the runtime, not fabricated by the UI: idle, running, resumed state, etc.
Your mock contract should add:
SessionStatus
- Idle
- Running
- WaitingForApproval
- WaitingForInput
- Completed
- Failed
- Aborted
This is better than inferring state only from the local UiPhase.
3. Checkpoints and diff projection
The SDK contains explicit checkpoint comparison support and a dedicated checkpoint-diff implementation.
For the UI contract:
CheckpointDescriptor
checkpoint_id
created_at
workspace_revision
changed_files
and events:
CheckpointCreated
CheckpointComparisonReady
CheckpointRestoreRequested
CheckpointRestoreBlocked
CheckpointRestored
Important: the UI should only request/display restore. LBE owns whether restore is permitted.
4. Running-command progress
This is a strong one.
The current SDK architecture has structured stdout/stderr streaming for commands and preserves the session/tool-call/tool IDs across the event pipeline.
Add:
CommandStarted
CommandStdoutDelta
CommandStderrDelta
CommandCompleted
CommandFailed
with:
tool_call_id
command_id
exit_code
This would make the terminal activity view considerably better than a generic ToolOutput.
5. Proceed-while-running / detached commands
The repo also explicitly supports a command continuing after the interactive tool call returns, with bounded logs and later inspection.
For LBE UI:
CommandDetached
DetachedCommandProgress
DetachedCommandCompleted
DetachedLogAvailable
Potential UI:
/processes
This is useful for builds, dev servers, watchers, tests, etc.
No process ownership should live in the TUI.
6. Context compaction lifecycle
There is an explicit context-compaction system in the repo.
You already show context usage. Add the missing lifecycle:
ContextCompactionSuggested
ContextCompactionStarted
ContextCompactionCompleted
ContextCompactionFailed
and snapshot fields:
context_used
context_capacity
context_percent
compaction_available
compaction_state
This makes /compact a proper typed UI contract rather than a placeholder.
7. Retry / mistake budget
The CLI exposes a configurable maximum consecutive retry/mistake count.
A neutral LBE UI contract could expose:
retry_count
retry_limit
and:
RetryScheduled
RetryLimitReached
Useful for showing why an agent stopped.
8. Runtime timeout
The CLI also has an explicit session timeout.
Add:
timeout_seconds
elapsed_seconds
plus:
TimeoutWarning
TimedOut
Again, runtime owns enforcement; UI only displays.
9. Diagnostic / health surface
The CLI has a dedicated doctor command for diagnosing configuration/runtime problems.
You already planned provider health, but I would add a more general:
/doctor
projection contract:
DiagnosticCheck
- id
- category
- status
- message
- remediation_available
Categories:
runtime
provider
workspace
tools
MCP
storage
credentials
terminal
This could become very useful later.
10. Hooks lifecycle
The repo has an explicit hook engine/contracts and CLI hook injection.
Your earlier reference mentioned hooks, but the typed UI lifecycle is still missing.
Add:
HookRegistered
HookStarted
HookCompleted
HookFailed
HookBlocked
and a mock /hooks view.
11. Plugin lifecycle, not just plugin listing
The SDK architecture explicitly includes plugin discovery/loading as a core responsibility. The CLI also supports plugin installation and management.
For LBE UI contract:
PluginDescriptor
plugin_id
name
version
source
state
capabilities
tools
states:
Discovered
Disabled
Loading
Ready
Failed
Do not make the TUI the plugin loader.
12. Schedules / automation lifecycle
The current repo has scheduled-runtime services and task infrastructure, and the CLI exposes schedule.
Add mock contracts:
ScheduleDescriptor
schedule_id
task
cadence
enabled
next_run
last_run
last_status
events:
ScheduleCreated
ScheduleUpdated
ScheduleTriggered
ScheduleRunStarted
ScheduleRunCompleted
ScheduleRunFailed
13. Subagent/team provenance
The architecture explicitly distinguishes session initiation modes such as:
user
automation
subagent
team
and persists child-session lineage.
That suggests adding:
SessionOrigin
parent_session_id
root_session_id
agent_id
team_id
This is better than adding a standalone “subagent panel” without lineage.
14. Aggregate usage
For shared/team sessions, the architecture distinguishes root-session usage from aggregate usage.
Later UI contract:
UsageSnapshot
input_tokens
output_tokens
cached_tokens
estimated_cost
root_usage
aggregate_usage
This also fits your provider-neutral architecture.
15. Generated media / artifact events
The current SDK architecture has a generic generated-media contract supporting image/audio/video/file-like outputs and artifact-backed sources.
Even though the current terminal is primarily coding-oriented, it is useful to future-proof:
ArtifactAvailable
GeneratedMediaAvailable
with:
artifact_id
media_type
mime_type
display_name
source_kind
The terminal could show:
[artifact] screenshot.png
[file] report.json
[audio] transcript.wav
without trying to render unsupported media inline.
Areas I would not carry over
These are Cline-specific or unnecessary for your intended boundary:
Cline auth
Cline API gateway
Cline Hub branding/protocol as product dependency
Cline account
Cline remote config
Cline telemetry implementation
Cline plugin package format
Cline data-directory naming
Cline-specific command permission format
The concepts can inform LBE contracts, but the ownership and identifiers should remain LBE-native.
